newsitem.title: FRANCE: French guide restores top rating to two kitchens.
newsitem.headline: French guide restores top rating to two kitchens.

text.p: The Gault-Millau restaurant guide to France named Jacques Chibois, chef and owner of La Bastide Saint Antoine restaurant in the southern French resort town of Grasse, its chef of the year on Tuesday.
The restaurant, which opened its doors just seven months ago, specialises in the cuisine of Provence and offers dinner without wine at about 380 to 600 francs ($75 to $120).
"This is a great honour, particularly since we have just opened," Chibois, who is 43, told Reuters.

"Our appeal is in the totality of our menu, which we change according to the seasons in order to please diners every time they return," said Chibois, who was previously chef at the Grey d'Albion luxury hotel in the Riviera city Cannes.

In its 1997 guide, released on Tuesday, Gault-Millau restored its highest rating to two restaurants which fell out of favour in last year's edition, but the overall number of top-rated kitchens remained at 12, the guide's authors said.

The latest Gault-Millau guide for France thus steered clear of the controversy triggered by last year's edition, which slashed the number of restaurants given its highest rating to a dozen from 30 after concluding that most were overrated.

The 1997 edition of the guide restored its coveted rating of four "toques" -- the traditional towering white chef's cap -- to Marc Meneau's L'Esperance in Saint-Pere-sous-Vezelay in central France and Alain Passard's L'Arpege in Paris. The two had been dropped into lower categories in the 1996 edition.

Two other super-chefs -- Joel Robuchon in Paris and Pierre Gagnaire in Saint-Etienne, central France -- were dropped from the top category because they had closed down, leaving a dozen restaurants in the highest category for a second year.
Gault-Millau said it gave special emphasis this year to moderately priced restaurants offering diners good value for their money.

The French restaurant industry's enduring financial crisis "has brought to the fore a new generation of chefs who know how to provide creative cooking at good value," the guide's editors said in a statement.
"Today, young chefs born out of the crisis know that a bill of 150 to 200 francs ($30 to $40) does not prevent them from using their imagination," the editors said.

The most exclusive French restaurants have been badly shaken by tough financial times in recent years, forcing them to cut back on costs, sell processed foods and kitchenware on the side or open cheaper bistros next door in order to remain afloat.
Gagnaire in January became the first top-rated chef in France to be forced into bankruptcy. He has since announced plans to open a more modest restaurant in Paris.
Robuchon retired at age 51, turning over his Paris restaurant to chef Alain Ducasse, who also runs the kitchen at the Louis XV in Monaco.

The rival Michelin guide, France's most prestigious restaurant guide, bestowed its highest award of three stars to 19 restaurants last year, down from 20 in 1995. Both L'Esperance and L'Arpege were included in Michelin's list of three-star restaurants in 1996.
Michelin's 1997 edition is due out early next year.
